lines: In this episode, self defence and private defence.
You must be able to explain the requirements for using lethal force, and your formative exam asks for them.

scenes.heading: Defending a life
bullets: Force, including lethal force, may be used in defence
A person preventing an attack on another

lines.text: It is a well entrenched principle of our law that one can use force, including lethal force, in defence of oneself, or someone in whom you have a legal interest or obligation to protect.
A legal interest could be, for example, the right of a parent to protect their child.
Or a spouse to protect their spouse.
Or a person preventing an attack on another.

scenes.definition: Someone you have an obligation to protect: a family member, or a third party being attacked by a criminal.
lines: The book defines a legal interest as someone that you have an obligation to protect.
Such as a family member.
Or a third party, such as a member of the public who is being attacked by a criminal, and you have no relationship to that third party.

scenes.heading: Constitutional principles
bullets: 10.1 Everybody has the right to life
10.3 Right to human dignity, equality and freedom
10.5 The highest right is the right to life
lines: In exercising your rights of self defence or private defence, the requirements of constitutionality must always be borne in mind.

lines.text: First, everybody has the right to life, including a criminal.
Second, all persons are presumed innocent until found guilty by a competent court or tribunal.
Third, everyone has the right to human dignity, equality and freedom.
Fourth, everyone has the right to own property.
Fifth, there is quite clearly a simple hierarchy in these rights, with the highest right being the right to life.

lines: This right applies to both victim and criminal.

scenes.definition: "Were the actions in doing so reasonable and justifiable in an open and democratic society based on principles of human dignity, equality and freedom?"
lines: In determining whether a person acted correctly in self defence, in taking another human's life, this is the test.
Were the actions in doing so reasonable and justifiable in an open and democratic society, based on principles of human dignity, equality and freedom?
This may seem complicated, but in reality it is not.

scenes.heading: Private defence and self defence
bullets: Private defence: someone you have a legal interest in
Self defence: purely protection of oneself
The law makes no legal distinction
lines: Private defence allows you to defend and protect someone in whom you have a legal interest, such as your child, your spouse, or a third party.
Self defence is purely protection of oneself.
The law makes no legal distinction between the two.

scenes.heading: Requirements for use of lethal force
bullets: 12.1 An attack against you or a third party, and it must be unlawful
12.2 Against a person, a threat to life, not property
12.3 About to start, or already begun
lines: These constitutional principles exist to prevent the unlawful taking of one human life by another, without legal justification.
You can injure or kill somebody in private defence or self defence if, bearing these principles in mind, the following legal requirements are present.

lines.text: One. There must be an attack against you, or a third party whom you are trying to protect from such an attack, and such attack must be unlawful.
Two. The attack must be against a person, that is, a threat to life, and not property.
Three. The attack must be about to start, or must already have begun.

rule.text: The attack must be against a person, and not property.

lines: The book underlines the words, not property.
The attack must be a threat to life, and not to property.

scenes.heading: Your defence must be absolutely necessary
bullets: 13.2 No other means to avoid the attack
13.3 Objectively reasonable, directed at the attacker
lines: In acting to defend such a person's life, your defence must be absolutely necessary to prevent or stop the attack.

lines.text: First, you cannot pre-emptively kill someone to stop an attack when that attack is not imminent or about to start.

lines: You cannot kill someone now to prevent an attack later.

lines.text: Second, you could not use any other means to avoid the attack.

lines: In the book's words, flight is better than fight.

lines.text: Third, the manner in which you defend yourself, or that other person, must be objectively reasonable under the circumstances.

lines: And your defence must be directed at the person making the attack, and not someone else.
For example, you cannot shoot an attacker's accomplice to prevent an attack.
You can only use force against the attacker.

rule.text: If you can avoid the use of force, you have a legal obligation to do so.

lines: Remember, if you can avoid the use of force, you have a legal obligation to do so.
The law requires that if you can avoid a confrontation, you must take reasonable steps to do so, for example by leaving the scene, if escape is possible.
If you do not try to escape when it is possible, it may be argued that you contributed towards the confrontation.
And therefore, that your actions in using force were not legally justifiable.

scenes.question: Which is a requirement for using lethal force?
options: The attack is against your property
The attack is unlawful, and about to start or already begun
You expect an attack some time later
lines: Your formative exam asks you to explain the legal requirements for using lethal force.
So, which of these is a requirement?
reveal: The attack must be unlawful, and it must be about to start or must already have begun.
It must be against a person, not property, and you cannot kill someone now to prevent an attack later.

scenes.question: Does the law treat private defence differently from self defence?
options: No, it makes no legal distinction
lines: One more.
Does the law treat private defence differently from self defence?
reveal: No. The law makes no legal distinction between the two.
Private defence protects someone you have a legal interest in, and self defence is purely protection of oneself.

points: Legal interest: someone you must protect
The right to life is the highest right
No legal distinction: private and self defence
Unlawful attack, on a person, about to start or begun
Avoid force if you can: flight is better than fight
lines: So, a legal interest is someone you have an obligation to protect.
The highest right is the right to life, for victim and criminal.
The law makes no legal distinction between private and self defence.
The attack must be unlawful, against a person, and about to start or already begun.
Your defence must be absolutely necessary, and directed at the attacker.
And if you can avoid the use of force, you have a legal obligation to do so.
